pages.name: One time constant
pages.text: A capacitor charged to 10 V empties through a resistor. The current is the voltage left ÷ R, so the fall slows as the voltage does; the dashed line is its pace now. The bar is the gap still to close. In one [[time constant]], written τ, it keeps 0.368 of itself. Here `τ = R × C = 47 s`, so 10 V becomes 3.68 V at 1τ, 1.35 V at 2τ and 0.50 V at 3τ. Drag the time handle.

A dotted line shows the pace now: kept up, it would reach the bottom one tau later. 3.68 V. From 0 to 1 tau, times 0.368. 1.35 V. From 1 to 2 tau, times 0.368. 0.50 V. From 2 to 3 tau, times 0.368. The time handle at 3 tau. Gap left at 3 tau, 141 s: 0.050 of the start.

pages.name: Two time constants
pages.task: After one time constant the capacitor is at 3.68 V. What is it after two?
pages.why: The second time constant takes the same share as the first, so the bar keeps 0.368 of what is left, `3.68 × 0.368 ≈ 1.35 V`. That is `10 × e^(−2)`. Equal stretches of time take the same share, not the same number of volts.

pages.name: R and C set the pace
pages.text: A bigger R lets less current through, and a bigger C must lose more charge for each volt. Together the voltage falls at `v ÷ RC` volts a second. The dashed line is the starting pace, `10 V ÷ 47 s`: kept up, it would empty the capacitor in exactly one RC. It slows as it falls, so it only gets to 0.368. That is why RC is the unit of time. As a rule, `v = V e^(−t/RC)`. After 30 s, `e^(−30/47) ≈ 0.528`, so 5.28 V. Slide R and C.

pages.name: 400 V after 10 s
pages.task: A 400 V capacitor empties through a resistor, with RC = 20 s. What is its voltage after 10 s?
pages.why: Count the time in time constants first, `10 ÷ 20 = 0.5`. Then `400 × e^(−0.5)` ≈ 243 V on the eˣ key. Half a time constant has not yet brought it down to 0.368 of the start.

pages.text: Now charge it from a 10 V supply. The charging current is the gap up to the supply ÷ R, so that gap shrinks just as the discharge voltage did, keeping 0.368 of itself each τ. pages.name: Charging, two time constants
pages.task: Charging from a 10 V supply, the capacitor is at 6.32 V after one time constant. What is it after two?
pages.why: The gap to the supply keeps 0.368 of itself each τ, so it goes 10 V, then 3.68 V, then 1.35 V. The capacitor is at `10 − 1.35 = 8.65 V`, 86.5% charged. The second τ closes 0.632 of a smaller gap.

pages.name: Never quite full
pages.text: At 4τ the gap left is `0.368^4 ≈ 0.018` of the start, so it is 98.2% charged. At 5τ it is `0.368^5 ≈ 0.007`, so 99.3%. By the rule the gap only ever shrinks, so it is never quite full. A trade tutorial counts 5τ as fully charged: a line people draw, not a point the curve reaches. The magnifier shows the 0.07 V still to go. Switch to discharging to see it from 400 V.

pages.name: 400 V after five
pages.task: A capacitor charged to 400 V empties for five time constants. What voltage is left?
pages.why: Five time constants keep `e^(−5)` of the start, so `400 × e^(−5)` ≈ 2.7 V is still there. 5τ is the usual line for empty, yet by the rule the gap never closes. Time alone never makes a capacitor safe, so prove it dead with a tester before you touch it.

pages.name: Cooling
pages.text: A hot part cooling in a room follows much the same curve. [[Newton's law of cooling]] says it cools at a rate proportional to the gap between its temperature and the room's, like the charging current. So the gap to the room keeps much the same share in each τ. It is a rougher fit: for heat given off as radiation, the law holds only for small temperature differences. Here a 90 °C part sits in a 20 °C room, with τ = 10 minutes.

pages.name: After 10 minutes
pages.task: This part starts at 90 °C in a 20 °C room, with a time constant of 10 minutes. What does it read after 10 minutes?
pages.why: The 70 °C gap to the room keeps 0.368 of itself in one time constant, `70 × 0.368 ≈ 25.8 °C`. The part reads the room plus the gap, `20 + 25.8 = 45.8 °C`. Then 29.5 °C at 20 minutes and 23.5 °C at 30, closing on the room but never passing it.

pages.name: 5 V for 100 s
pages.task: A 5 V supply charges 470 µF through 100 kΩ. What is the capacitor's voltage after 100 s?
pages.why: RC is `100,000 × 0.000470 = 47 s`, so 100 s is `100 ÷ 47 ≈ 2.13` time constants. The gap keeps `e^(−2.13) ≈ 0.119` of the 5 V, about 0.60 V, so the capacitor is at `5 − 0.60 = 4.40 V`.

pages.name: Oil after 40 minutes
pages.task: Oil at 80 °C cools in a 30 °C room, with a time constant of 20 minutes. What is it after 40 minutes?
pages.why: 40 minutes is two time constants. The 50 °C gap to the room keeps `e^(−2) ≈ 0.135` of itself, about 6.8 °C, so the oil reads `30 + 50 × e^(−2)` ≈ 36.8 °C.
